Title: Financial stability nets - complementing and reinforcing micro and macro perspectives
Subtitle: Speech by Mr Mario Bergara, Governor of the Central Bank of Uruguay, at the opening of the 9th meeting of the IADI Latin America Regional Committee (LARC), Punta del Este, 21 March 2012.
text: Mario Bergara: Financial stability nets  complementing and reinforcing micro and macro perspectives Speech by Mr Mario Bergara, Governor of the Central Bank of Uruguay, at the opening of the 9th meeting of the IADI Latin America Regional Committee (LARC), Punta del Este, 21 March 2012. * * * The speech is based on an article prepared by Messrs Mario Bergara, Gerardo Licandro and Jorge Ponce for the Conference Macroprudential policies to achieve financial stability, hosted by the Central Bank of Uruguay and the International Monetary Fund, Punta del Este, 29 February  2 March 2012. The views expressed herein are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the view of the Banco Central del Uruguay. 1. Lessons from the crisis: What is new? The aftermath of the 2008 global financial crisis witnessed a surge on the discussion of financial stability issues. In some countries the focus of the debate is on the role of the shadow financial system, its relationship with banks, and the regulatory and supervisory failure to address the problem of regulatory arbitrage. In Europe, the main concerns lies on the lack of a European safety net, mainly due to the absence of a European lender of last resort. In emerging countries, however, the discussion is centered around the impact of the crisis on the volatility of capital flows and the architecture of the international financial system. Though some of the phenomena underlying the origins and depth of the financial crisis were either new or located in new instruments and markets, most of the issues that were raised during this episode can be traced back to the first financial crisis of the world. In the following lines, we develop the argument that even though financial stability concerns are as old as financial systems, and despite some of the main lessons of the recent crisis look pretty much alike the lessons of several financial episodes of the past (to which many jurisdictions have already reacted), there are good reasons to heighten our concern with financial stability. Financial stability arises as a main concern, despite the fact that the concept is neither new, nor the main explanation for the collapse the world experienced in 2008. The crisis revealed the existence of regulatory failures at different levels, as well as problems in the design of the financial safety nets both at the national and international level. In what appears to be nearly a paradox, regulatory failure has remained in the background overshadowed by the concentration of policy making bodies in financial stability. Financial stability concerns have had an impact on the management of both macro and micro policies regarding financial stability for a long time now. Uruguay can give examples of that matter. To quote one, in 1998 when facing a bullish international environment, Uruguay increased capital requirements on banks to tame the seemingly bubbling behaviour of domestic credit. For years now, Uruguay has worked on increasing the maturity of domestic public debt to avoid liquidity pressures on fiscal accounts that might in the end affect the health of the banking sector. Another example is our countrys concern with real exchange appreciations. In the graph below it is possible to see that every financial crisis we had in the last 50 year was preceded by a deep and gradual appreciation of the real exchange rate followed by a sudden and sharp depreciation. That lesson has carved deep into the skins of the Uruguayan people, who see the appreciation of the currency as a sign of trouble to come. As a reflection of that concern, macroeconomic policy has always been keen to keep an eye on the exchange rate market, trying to prevent the misalignment of the real exchange rate with respect to fundamentals. Financial stability is then a long term concern in both macro en micro economic policy design. BIS central bankers speeches 1 Despite their long standing tradition on caring about financial stability, emerging countries like Uruguay are paying a renewed and closer attention to the matter because the international environment has changed. The G20 solution to the financial crisis has set clearly the boundaries of the international financial safety net, which were previously unknown, and has left a legacy of medium term excess liquidity that has to be dealt with in emerging economies. The sum of those two elements implies much more volatile international capital flows, in an international financial architecture in which each country is basically on its own. As a result, even though financial stability is nothing new to us, we are paying a much closer look at the ways to complementing and reinforcing efforts to enhance the stability of our financial system and its contribution to the whole economy. In the next lines we would go over the way we envisage financial stability in the new international context. 2. Why is public intervention in financial markets necessary? Public intervention in an industry is commonly justified by the existence of market failures and externalities. Market failures and externalities are particularly pregnant in financial markets. Financial markets operate in an environment of asymmetric information where adverse selection, moral hazard and costly state verification problems play a very important role. Moreover, the activities of the financial market players pose important spill-overs and externalities over other players in the industry, other industries, the domestic economy and even spread over other economies. Many examples of contagion, externalities and other market failures may be identified on the recent global financial crisis. Some aspects that are specific to the financial industry provide a rationale for public intervention in financial markets: Representing and protecting small claimholders. Financial institutions (e.g. banks) finance risky investments (e.g. loans) through retail deposits and other liabilities. Retail depositors, as well as other claimholders, are relatively small (and maybe nonsophisticated) agents. They do not have either the technical capabilities or the incentive to monitor financial institutions. Hence, public intervention is justified in order to cope with the potential moral hazard problem. In particular, a public entity assumes the representation of small claimholders of financial institutions in order to protect them (see Dewatripont and Tirole, 1994). Controlling systemic risk, financial and macroeconomic stability. One of the main functions of financial institutions is to manage risks. For this reason, financial institutions are inherently fragile, to the point that some authors refer to them as risk machines (see Bessis, 2010). Moreover, troubles in one institution may rapidly amplify and spread to others through balance sheet interlinks and financial contagion, and affect the payment systems and the real economy (see, for instance, Allen and Gale 2000, Diamond and Dybvig 1983, Freixas et al. 2000. Ponce and Tubio 2010 offer a review of the literature). In addition to these externalities, amplification and spill-over effects, a situation of financial instability may be the result of the materialization of a macroeconomic risk which is common to all financial institutions (see Rochet, 2004). Yet, financial institutions may face difficulties to coordinate actions in order to resolve potentially damaging imbalances. Rochet and Vives (2004) demonstrate in a formal model that such coordination failure may determine that solvent financial institutions face severe liquidity shortfalls. Hence, these market failures and the need to preserve public goods (e.g. the payment system and the financial and macroeconomic stability) provide another rationale for public intervention. Protecting taxpayers money. Financial crises have demonstrated to impose large cleaning burdens to fiscal authorities. Hence, the protection of fiscal revenues is another rationale for prompt public intervention in order to reduce the frequency and the impact of crises, and to quickly and efficiently resolve them once they have materialized. 2 BIS central bankers speeches Public intervention in financial markets commonly implies a series of functions that can be classified into the categories of prevention and resolution. Among the category of prevention one can mention the activities of monitoring and assessing risks (two crucial functions of financial supervision), and the application of a regulatory policy. A regulatory policy implies the use of rules (i.e. regulations) but also of preventive action (e.g. to enforce rules), and corrective action (e.g. to lean against imbalances). The resolution policy involves the use of rules, which are important to guarantee prompt and efficient resolution processes, the resolution and cleaning of institutions in trouble, and the correction of imbalances. Many tools are used to fulfil the objectives of public intervention in financial markets: prudential regulation, control and supervision (i.e. preventive tools), and resolution mechanisms and emergency liquidity assistance (i.e. resolution tools). The set of all these functions and tools provides a financial safety net to the financial system. In general, the functions and tools of the financial safety net are allocated to different agencies. For example, it is generally the central bank which is responsible for the provision of emergency liquidity assistance. Other responsibilities like prudential regulation, supervision, and deposit insurance are allocated inside the central bank in some jurisdictions and outside in others. In order to determine the most efficient governance structure for the financial safety net policymakers should consider the agencies explicit conflict of objectives, the potential conflict of opinions about key issues (e.g. the intervention or the liquidation of a financial institution, the provision of short term emergency assistance, the authorization of mergers and acquisitions), and the need for coordination. In addition to this, policymakers should consider the pros and cons of the unification versus the separation of financial safety net agencies on the grounds of their relative expertise, capabilities, reputation, credibility and institutional strength. Moreover, the financial safety net affects and is affected by other functions like the conduction of monetary policy and fiscal policy. These effects should also be considered when designing financial stability institutions. We come back to this point in Section 5. 3. Micro- and macro-prudential perspectives Sound risk management are needed not only at individual institutions but also at the financial system as a whole. The severity of the recent global financial crisis can only be explained by the systemic risk factors that propagated the problems in individual institutions and markets to the entire global financial system. The close relationship between individual and systemic risks provides a rationale for complementing the traditional micro-prudential perspective (focusing on individual risks) with a macroprudential perspective (assessing systemic risks). Most of the financial regulatory and supervisory apparatus focalizes on the microprudential perspective. Some exceptions are the cases of Spain and Uruguay which have been implementing mechanisms to control both the static and the dynamic dimensions of systemic risk (e.g. dynamic provisioning and limit to currency mismatches) during the last decade. The recent Basel III capital and liquidity accord makes advances in the consideration of systemic risk. However, most of the current financial regulation focuses on the stability of each financial institution and market considered in isolation. Hence, it largely ignores the externalities that one institution poses on the others, the systemic importance of individual institutions, and the risks that are generated endogenously to the financial system. Moreover, the regulation focusing on individual institutions may open possibilities for regulatory arbitrage, i.e. the possibility that financial institutions avoid regulations of certain activities by conducting them through other entities (or lines of business) which are subject to less severe regulations. The final objective of the macro-prudential perspective is to avoid the materialization of large social and economic costs due to financial instabilities. Hence, this perspective to financial stability considers the entire financial system and intends to protect their infrastructures (e.g. the payment system, the interbank and the money markets). The macro-prudential BIS central bankers speeches 3 perspective oversights the aggregate risk of the entire financial system by explicitly considering the exposition of individual institutions and market to common sources of risk, and the dynamic of risks that are generated endogenously. The micro- and the macro-prudential perspectives should be jointly considered in order to avoid regulatory arbitrage and to ensure financial stability. Both perspectives should complement and reinforce each other in order to protect small customers and the stability of the entire financial system. Hence, their contribution should be transversal to the financial safety net agencies rather than the responsibility of a specific, macroprudential authority. The following sections analyse the implications of jointly considering the micro- and the macroprudential perspectives on rules, institutions, governance and the design of macroeconomic policy. 4. Micro- and macro prudential policies: A two-way road The following lines we argue that the function of financial stability implies a more articulated cooperation between institutions concerned with macro and microeconomic policy making and regulation. 4.1 Implications of systemic risk on traditionally micro-prudential rules and institutions The consideration of systemic risks (e.g. exposure to common and correlated risks, interconnectedness, financial and real sector conglomerates, cross border issues, regulatory arbitrage, new kinds of risks and developments) have implications on traditionally microprudential rules and institutions. Risk-based regulation. Risk-based regulation implies that similar risks face similar regulations regardless the financial institution and activity that generate them. This kind of regulation is a direct way to provide safety and protection to claimholders of financial institutions and other participants to the financial system. Other kind of regulation (e.g. activity-based and institution-based) may imply that important sources of risk remain unregulated and foster regulatory arbitrage. Moreover, they may ignore the important synergies, interlinks and externalities among different activities and financial institutions (which are particularly relevant under financial conglomerates) that contribute to systemic risk. To anticipate and control excessive risk taking is a direct mechanism to mitigate the negative effects that the materialization of risks impose to the stability of the financial system. A risk-based regulation acts directly over the incentives to take risks, and reduces the possibility of regulatory gaps whereby important activities that should be regulated escape regulation. Dynamic regulatory perimeter. Financial institutions are special not only because they are specialized on risk management but also because they have shown to be creative and efficient on the development of new products. Financial innovation may contribute to social welfare but it also may serve as a device to arbitrate regulation and thereby to increase individual and aggregate risk. The capacity to innovate of financial institutions, the potential for regulatory arbitrage, and their potentially dangerous effects to the whole financial system provide a rationale for allowing the agencies on the financial safety net to expand and contract the regulatory perimeter (i.e. to select what institutions and activities should be regulated) in order to promptly react to new kinds of risks as market develop. The possibility to dynamically adjust the regulatory perimeter is also justified by the trend of financial institutions to form groups and conglomerates where a stockholding company (even a non-financial one) owns financial institutions. Moreover, state-owned and privately-owned financial institutions managing similar risks should be in the same side of the regulatory perimeter and then subject to the same kind of regulations and controls. 4 BIS central bankers speeches Uruguay represents a particular case in Latin America where the Law gives powers to the financial sector regulator and supervisor to adjust the regulatory perimeter in order to fulfil its mandate of preserving the stability of the financial system. Centralized regulation. The regulation of financial institutions should be centralized in a unique regulator. The existence of many agencies regulating the same financial institution (e.g. in an activity-based regulatory framework) may imply important overlaps in regulatory requirements or important gaps where important activities that should be regulated escape regulation. Moreover, financial markets are naturally dynamic and financial institutions and markets (e.g. banks and other intermediaries, pension funds, insurance and capital markets) show important interlinks which justify the need for a large level of consistency thought different regulations. More centralization of financial regulation may imply lower bureaucratic costs, economies of scale and scope, the use of a conglomerates logic and lower regulatory arbitrage. These advantages from concentrating financial regulation may be traded off the potential advantages from a less concentrated financial regulation (e.g. efficiency gains due to specialization). The rules and tools used by the centralized regulator should consider micro- and macroprudential risks. Otherwise stated, the financial regulator should take both prudential perspectives into consideration when writing rules and using regulatory tools and instruments. Hence, the financial regulator should receive as a clear and explicit mandate not only to ensure the stability of individual institutions and markets, but also to guarantee the stability of the whole financial system. Other aspects that are related to the governance of the financial regulator and its relationship with other agencies are analysed in Section 5. 4.2 Implications of micro-prudential concerns on macroeconomic polices Micro prudential policy has a direct impact on macroeconomic policy, but experience shows that the reciprocal is also true. Changes in regulation and supervision affect the power, reach and timing of macro policies. Leaving aside the obvious effects in crisis times, it is well known the impact of regulation and supervision on the development of financial markets and credit. Changes on the development of financial markets have a direct effect on the power of monetary policy. Changes in credit affect might affect consumption and therefore fiscal revenues. The recent crisis has highlighted the potential effect of failure in regulation and supervision on the creation of asset price bubbles. If we add those normal time effects to the ones generated during times of stress, we have a clear case why both monetary and fiscal policy should be concerned with financial stability. Nevertheless, since many financial crisis can be traced back to problems in policy at the macro level, there is a clear case of a reciprocal concern on macro policy design coming from the authorities of the financial safety net. Particularly in the case of emerging economies, threats to financial stability come from the macro environment, and depend largely on the way macroeconomic policy is conducted. Reinhardt and Rogoff illustrate that financial crisis tend to cluster in history, and are related to the volatility of capital inflows and commodity prices. The literature on early warning systems suggest that the most basic features that currency and banking crisis seem to share are unsustainable appreciations of the domestic currency and fiscal problems. In the case of Uruguay, the three cases depicted in the figure portrayed in section I can be explained by (or cannot be understood without) problems on the design of macroeconomic policy. Since most financial crisis events have macroeconomic factors that either caused or amplified them, financial stability concerns should affect the design of macroeconomic policies. The impact of macroeconomic policies on financial stability justifies the presence of macro policy makers in the discussion of financial stability issues not only as the ones that pay the BIS central bankers speeches 5 bill once the crisis has started, but also as key actors in the prevention of episodes of financial instability. A direct result of the line of reasoning that this paper develops is that financial stability is a two way road, in which all the actors involved have some milage to cover in order to ensure financial stability. 5. Financial stability committees: from safety to stability nets The final outcome in terms of financial stability depends on the policies conducted by several of the agencies that are involved on macroeconomic policy design and the financial safety net: prudential regulation and supervision, emergency liquidity assistance, deposit insurance, etc. All the agencies that may contribute to the stability of a financial system own policy instruments and tools, and are responsible for their use. The challenges are that all these agencies should internalize the effects of their policies on financial stability; that all these agencies should complement each other on the identification and the assessment of risks and vulnerabilities; and that policy instruments and tools should be used and calibrated by considering both the micro- and the macro-prudential perspectives to financial stability. Operationally independent agencies should receive clear mandates and remain accountable for the outcome of their policies. Hence, safety net agencies should receive the mandate of contributing to the stability of the whole financial system in addition to their specific mandates. Yet, agencies may have conflicting opinions on crucial decisions which may end in situations of financial instability. Financial stability committees appear as a response to align incentives, coordinate efforts, and contribute for all agencies to comply with their respective mandates. Financial stability committees also add to the financial safety net by helping the micro- and the macroprudential perspectives to complement and to reinforce each other. Financial stability committees are a step toward financial stability nets. Uruguay, like other Latin American countries, has recently created a committee with the objectives of sharing information and coordinating actions among the financial safety net agencies. Financial stability committees serve as a framework to share information and to coordinate actions. They also help to improve the identification and the assessment of risks, and the accountability of the stability net agencies. Hence, they help safety net agencies to comply with their mandates. The specific mandates of safety net agencies and the operational constraints that they face imply that each of them specializes on the oversight of specific dimensions of financial risks. To share, combine and analyse the different pieces of information under the leadership of a financial stability committee improves the efficiency of risk assessment not only by profiting from the specialization of safety nets agencies on assessing specific risks, but also by having a more comprehensive approach to risks, by considering the interlinks between them, and by anticipating new risks. To get information from different safety net agencies also has the benefit for the financial stability committee (and the social welfare) of reducing the potential that the industry captures safety net agencies (see Boyer and Ponce, 2011). Moreover, the sharing of information, the insights provided by different safety net agencies, and the explicit consideration of different point of view on crucial decisions imply the generation of observable (and verifiable) information which may improve the accountability of the agencies. Title: Uruguay is prepared for the challenges posed by the international volatility scenario, affirmed the president of the BCU
text: December 16 Uruguay is prepared for challenges posed by the scenario of international volatility, said the president of the BCU Uruguay is prepared from the point of view of risk management in the face of a volatile international context, said the president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara. The president of the monetary institution spoke with the government's economic team at the Economic Forum of the Christian Association of Business Leaders (ACDE). "If accidents appear in the world, Uruguay is in a position to cope with them," according to the hypothesis formulated by Bergara exhibiting a risk assessment map of the country's economy. In that sense, he reiterated that the interventions of the BCU in the exchange market aim to soften external shocks in the face of the international volatility of the dollar and specified that it also allowed to reduce by 5,000 million dollars the stock of Monetary Regulation Bills. When reviewing the international context that affects Uruguay as an economy open to the world, he mentioned the expectation for the rise in interest rates in the United States, the growth at lower rates of China that, despite the fall in investment, it will demand food of the type that Uruguay exports. "It is natural to think that we are on the way to normalization of international conditions," because "rates in the U.S. were not going to be zero for a lifetime, China was not going to always grow at 11% and, therefore, it is decent that it now expands to 8%." Stressed. Bergara also referred to the forecasts of a fall in Brazil's economy and showed optimism about the changes in Argentina regarding the dismantling of trade policy that implied restrictions on Uruguayan trade. Given this scenario, the president of the BCU emphasized that Uruguay is well prepared. "The Uruguayan economy and society are actually different from 11 years ago and this is not the result of an economic policy on autopilot," he said. However, he indicated that international volatility brings as a challenge inflationary pressures for which contractionary monetary policy is necessary. "The explicit goals of growth of the amount of money have been met" in the same way that "domestic demand begins to slow down, adapting to the new reality," added the president of the BCU. Bergara's presentation was called "Economic Policy Challenges in a New Global and Regional Scenario" and was made at the Forum in which the Minister of Economy and Finance, Danilo Astori; the Undersecretary of that portfolio, Pablo Ferreri; the director of the Macroeconomic Advisor, Andres Masoller and the director of the Office of Planning and Budget, alvaro Garcia. Title: The new president of the Central Bank of Uruguay took office
text: 28 November 2018 The new president of the Central Bank of Uruguay took office Alberto Grana assumed as president of the Central Bank of Uruguay, who served to date and since 2006 as manager of Economic Policy and Markets; and that between January 2014 and April 2015 also was president of the BCU. The inauguration ceremony took place in the Enrique V. Iglesias Room and was attended by the Minister of Economy and Finance, Danilo Astori; the vice president of the BCU -until today in exercise of the presidency-, Jorge Gamarra; the director of the BCU, Washington Ribeiro; the general secretary of the BCU, Elizabeth Oria; and the former president of the BCU, Mario Bergara. Both Jorge Gamarra and Washington Ribeiro highlighted Grana's skills for the position, stressing that he has already shown that he can do it "with great solvency", in reference to the previous period in which he held the position of president. Under the premise of giving the Bank "the place it deserves", Jorge Gamarra referred to the cultural change that the Bank has undergone in the last ten years, highlighting the participation, commitment and initiative of all employees as the most salient characteristics. In this regard, he said that the change was "the product of a collective work" and "of true teamwork." In reference to this period of time that he shared with the rest of the protagonists of the act of assumption, he also highlighted the way in which "a new management model based on strategic planning was consolidated" and from a five-year plan of which the goals elaborated by the different sections of the Bank are fully transversal. Gamarra also announced that in the coming days the BCU will be the first public body to certify all its processes in quality. In addition, he listed the awards and recognitions obtained by the Institution linked to transparency, good practices and access to information. In turn, the Minister of Economy and Finance, Danilo Astori, highlighted the intelligence of the BCU to face its relationship with the rest of the public sector. "It has been an independent bank but at the same time integrated," he said. The Secretary General, Elizabeth Oria, was in charge of reading the resolution of the President of the Republic that, with the corresponding permission of the Chamber of Senators, designates the president of the monetary authority. The new president, Alberto Grana, referred to the different issues related to the central bank tasks. "Uruguay is paradigmatic from the point of view of institutional coordination," he said, referring to aspects previously handled by Minister Astori. For Grana, the regional situation still awaits a roadmap . "Both the situation in Brazil and Argentina require constant monitoring," he said. Domestically, according to Grana, Uruguay has been able to "weather these situations." At the same time, he highlighted the country's strengths in terms of macroeconomic coordination. For the new president, it will also be necessary to deal with global challenges, fundamentally the trade war between the US and China, which generates constant uncertainty and volatility. With regard to the exchange rate, he was clear and forceful expressing that "we will not tolerate sudden changes" and that in all cases it must correspond to the fundamentals of the economy. Grana concluded by thanking the commitment of all the Bank's employees, which added to their institutional loyalty, allow them to take on this new challenge. For his part, the former president of the BCU, Mario Bergara, emphasized the link that the BCU has with society, based on transparency and the fulfillment of its tasks. "We are proud of the levels of reputation the Bank has," he said.

Title: A reflection on the transformation of the State in the framework of the 50 years of the BCU and the OPP
text: December 13, 2017 A reflection on the transformation of the State within the framework of the 50 years of the BCU and the OPP The president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara; together with the director of the Office of Planning and Budget (OPP), alvaro Garcia; They reflected on the process of reforming the State during a conference on the occasion of the fiftieth anniversary of the creation of both institutions. During his presentation, Bergara pointed out that the reform of the State is a process that has been going on for more than a decade in Uruguay and that is why he emphasized that there can be no talk of a single act. "The reform of the State encompasses organizational structures, incentive structures and forms of planning and control," said the president of the BCU. In that sense, Bergara reflected that in the last 12 years structural reforms were carried out that have to do with the way in which the State is organized for the Compliance with certain rules of the game. At the conference, the president of the BCU listed a list of relevant changes made that, he said, have transformed the structure of the State. Among those attending the meeting were the Minister of Economy and Finance, Danilo Astori; the Undersecretary of Economy and Finance, Pablo Ferreri; among other senior government officials, as well as authorities from the Central Bank of Uruguay and the Office of Planning and Budget. Title: Navigating in uncertainty requires understanding this world
text: ADM Lunch Mario Bergara: "Navigating uncertainty requires understanding this world" In the cycle of Working Lunches organized by the Association of Marketing Leaders (ADM) presented this Wednesday, July 26 , the president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara. The dissertation was entitled "Economic Policy in a New World: Unknowns and Capabilities ( ). The president of the BCU began by referring to the systematic challenges that arise in macroeconomic management from the constant reactions in a changing world. However, he explained that "the greater the volatility, the greater the exuberance of the financial markets" and that this requires special attention since it is necessary to discover what the real basis of that situation is. Given the uncertainty raised, Bergara calls for an economic policy approach that evaluates risks and with management capacity at different times. He argued that "in a global environment fraught with uncertainty," the stance should be "balanced goals and consistent budgets." He stressed that in this environment "the Uruguayan economy has behaved more than decently," even with a recent rebound. Bergara said that "in the current situation we have greater tranquility regarding inflation and the financial system, and greater concern regarding competitiveness." " Today we have an opportunity to influence inflation expectations. If we understand that we are in a lower inflation scenario, similar inflation expectations will help maintain current levels," he explained. He called on employers, price makers and workers to "fight together for expectations of low inflation." In turn, he pointed out that the BCU continues to be flexible with monetary policy, since global expectations about the dollar have conditioned capital flows and portfolio change. "We share the concern about the exchange rate arrears and we are so concerned that so far this year the BCU has bought more than 2 billion dollars . The competitiveness of companies is always present among the concerns and that is why this action, "he stressed. Bergara also referred to financial inclusion and stressed that "it has been received very healthily by society. Today payments through electronic means are almost 30% of the total." He added that "to continue clinging to cash and the check is to continue clinging to an expensive, inefficient, insecure world." "The Financial Inclusion Law is not only about giving orders, it is also negotiating with financial institutions things that used to charge and now do not charge," he said. Bergara took the opportunity to announce that in the coming months the BCU will apply a pilot plan for the issuance of digital banknotes. "To understand this new world driven by technological change is to have an agenda for society," he said. In this regard, he explained that technological change will generate structural transformations in society: obsolescence of jobs, businesses that do not own assets, markets organized through digital platforms, automation, among others. " Navigating uncertainty requires understanding this world," the BCU president concluded.

No obstante, explic que cuanto mayor volatilidad, mayor exuberancia de los mercados financieros y que eso requiere especial atencin ya que es necesario descubrir cul es la base real de esa situacin. Ante la incertidumbre planteada, Bergara reivindica un enfoque de poltica econmica que evale riesgos y con capacidad de manejo en los distintos momentos. Sostuvo que en un entorno global plagado de incertidumbre, la postura debe ser objetivos equilibrados y presupuestos consistentes. Destac que en este entorno la economa uruguaya se ha comportado ms que decentemente, incluso con un repunte reciente. Bergara indic que en la situacin actual tenemos mayor tranquilidad respecto a la inflacin y el sistema financiero, y mayor preocupacin respecto a la competitividad. Hoy tenemos una oportunidad de incidir en las expectativas de inflacin. Si entendemos que estamos en un escenario de inflacin ms baja, expectativas de inflacin similares ayudarn a mantener los niveles actuales, explic. Convoc a empresarios, formadores de precio y trabajadores a dar juntos la batalla por expectativas de una inflacin baja. A su vez, seal que el BCU contina siendo flexible con la poltica monetaria, ya que las expectativas globales sobre el dlar han condicionado los flujos de capital y el cambio de portafolios. La preocupacin por el atraso cambiario la compartimos y tanto nos preocupa que en lo que va del ao el BCU lleva comprados ms de 2000 millones de dlares. La competitividad de las empresas est siempre presente entre las preocupaciones y por eso este accionar, subray. Bergara se refiri tambin a la inclusin financiera y destac que ha sido recibida muy saludablemente por la sociedad. Hoy los pagos a travs de medios electrnicos son casi el 30% del total. Agreg que "seguir aferrados al efectivo y al cheque es seguir aferrados a un mundo caro, ineficiente, inseguro". "La ley de Inclusin Financiera no es solo dar rdenes, es tambin negociar con las instituciones financieras cosas que antes cobraban y ahora no cobran", recalc. Bergara aprovech la ocasin para anunciar que en los prximos meses el BCU aplicar un plan piloto para la emisin de billetes digitales. Entender este nuevo mundo impulsado por el cambio tecnolgico es tener una agenda para la sociedad, sostuvo. Al respecto explic que el cambio tecnolgico generar transformaciones estructurales en la sociedad: obsolescencia de empleos, negocios que no poseen activos, mercados organizados a travs de plataformas digitales, automatizacin, entre otras. Navegar en la incertidumbre requiere entender este mundo, concluy el presidente del BCU. Title: Encouraging the possibility of losing investment grade is irresponsible
text: August 28, 2018 Bergara: "Encouraging the possibility of losing investment grade is irresponsible" The president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara, analyzed the main challenges and opportunities facing the Uruguayan economy in a context of global and regional turbulence. The region promotes noise, not only because neighboring countries are affected by international prices and the fluctuation of the value of the dollar, but also because problems are added in the economic and political field, Bergara analyzed in an exhibition to which Attended this Tuesday, August 28, invited by the Association of Automotive Brand Dealers (ASCOMA). In his lecture, Bergara reflected on economic growth at decent rates, the recovery of domestic demand, the healthy evolution of exports of goods and services and the consistent current account surplus of the balance of payments. This occurs in an orderly fiscal framework, guided by the need for adaptation, with growth of the economy that still does not lead to improvements in employment levels. In that sense, Bergara highlighted the challenges for employment imposed by technological dynamics. "There are already robots that make decisions, read X-rays or make legal reports. This does not mean that these professionals will disappear, but that they will perform tasks that add more value," he analyzed. The best thing that can happen is that workers and employers can sit down in time to discuss the retraining processes. The State at the time generated institutions such as the National Institute of Employment and Vocational Training (INEFOP), which can collaborate in identifying threatened jobs and begin to retrain together with companies those workers whose positions are threatened, added the president of the Central Bank. Among other points, Bergara also stressed the need to reactivate the investment process as well as work to lower the fiscal deficit. From the point of view of the sustainability of public debt, he stressed that the levels of indebtedness and interest are manageable, but the deficit must be smoothed. "I find it very irresponsible that in this discussion about correcting the deficit, where we are not standing on the edge of the precipice much less, where we take advantage of the strengths of the economy to manage it, issues that are very expensive for society are encouraged. Uruguayan," he said at one section of his lecture. In this way, Bergara rejected the possibility that the country loses the investment grade and that this represents a problem for the next government administrations. "Uruguay is nowhere near losing the investment grade and (therefore) making noise that we are on the verge of losing the investment grade seems to us extremely irresponsible and unfair. And worse of all, what this implies is disregarded. Although ordinary people do not know how it affects them, we do know that it affects a lot, because it means whether one is going to be lent or not, under what conditions and, therefore, if they have the possibility of sustaining processes in the productive and social field. It's too important an issue to play for minor policy issues," he said. In this area, Bergara said that the vision of the rating agencies rules out such a possibility. Title: Technological changes do not modify the conceptual reasons why the financial system is regulated
text: September 5, 2018 Mario Bergara: "Technological changes do not change the conceptual reasons for why the financial system is regulated " The adaptation of financial systems to technological change was part of the line of reasoning of the president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara, during a conference he gave this Wednesday, September 5, invited to the Blockchain Summit Uruguay. During his presentation, Bergara made a retrospective to reflect on the fact that throughout history the financial world has adapted to technological developments. In that sense, the conference called "Challenges of central banks in the face of technological dynamics ( ) " was focused on the current disruptive process. "We do not have a vision that fintech will pass over the banking system, because the adaptability of traditional institutions has proven to be important," said the president of the BCU. In that sense, he urged to look at the coexistence of innovation with traditional institutions while the process of combination and competition between traditional agents and innovative platforms takes place. "You don't have to caricature the innovation process in terms of banks versus fintech or innovations versus traditional banks. The difference is in the speed, globality, complementarity and network effects, among others, which gives a different cut to the current process," he said. In this scenario, the president of the Central Bank emphasized that technological changes do not modify the conceptual reasons for why the financial system is regulated. "The protection of unsophisticated agents must continue to be taken care of more than ever as well as the prevention of systemic risks. We must understand what is happening now to, in any case, adapt the regulatory and control mechanisms to meet these objectives," he said. In this way, he recognized that the regulatory perimeter is expanding, electronic platforms generate opportunities in terms of access to services, financial inclusion and financing. "Regulating what should not be done can make innovations unfeasible; on the contrary, regulating what is due, makes the innovative process consistent with the security that the financial markets have to give," said Bergara. On the other hand, when referring to bitcoin and cryptocurrencies, he recalled that these are financial assets of very high volatility, which hardly constitute a threat in terms of currency. "They don't have the necessary features to replace currencies, nor the proper verification mechanisms. Rather, they operate as risky financial assets due to their volatility, with small magnitudes in transaction volume ," exemplified the president of the BCU. In turn, he said that at the academic level blockchain appears as a new organizational mechanism with market and hierarchical aspects, which is leveraged in terms of reducing transaction costs.

Title: The development strategy of the financial system is a factor of calm and not the epicenter of crisis
text: Mario Bergara: "The development strategy of the financial system is a factor of tranquility and not the epicenter of crisis" The president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara, reviewed the strengths of the Uruguayan economy to face the shocks coming from the international context. "At another time winds that were not stronger than the current one generated problems, because we did not have an adequate platform," said the president of the BCU, during his dissertation invited by the Official Spanish Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Navigation of Uruguay. In that sense, Bergara compared the current strengths of the Uruguayan economy with what happened in the years 1982 and 2002. Among them, he mentioned the decision to have a flexible exchange rate, the regulation of the banking system with an appropriate institutionality as well as the adequate debt management strategy . "The BCU's operations in the debt market have strengthened reserve levels by 7 billion over two years," he recalled. Likewise, the president of the BCU also ratified that the investment grade "is not in danger at all" in the current scenario. Bergara assured entrepreneurs that the risk management approach is a benchmark of economic policy. In that sense, he pointed out that fiscal adequacy measures mean reacting in time with political responsibility to the global context. "Correcting one percentage point of the output gap is preferable as a short-term measure, if that generates insurance for the future," he emphasized. The presentation of the president of the BCU, called "Economic cycles, external shocks and macroeconomic responsibility ( )", gaveor a vision on the most relevant aspects for Uruguay when facing the context of global uncertainty and volatility. Among other points, he noted the slim possibility of an increase in interest rates by the United States in the coming months; the reduction in the price of food, in his opinion more due to the effect of the behavior of the dollar than due to demand; political instability in Brazil and its impact on Uruguay, as well as macroeconomic signals from Argentina. Regarding this last aspect, the president of the BCU reflected that there is "macroeconomic tension", but because the changes seem to have a north, the markets are willing to grant a waiting time. On the Uruguayan economy, the president of the Central Bank said that consumption levels have a certain slowdown, but still validate high prices.

Title: Bergara ratified multiple objectives policy: We put more emphasis on some, but without drama
text: March 6, 2018 Bergara ratified a policy of multiple objectives: "We put greater emphasis on some, but without drama" The president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara, spoke to a hundred businessmen associated with the Official Spanish Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Navigation (CAMACOES) about the impact of global conditions on the Uruguayan economy and the economic policy approach to maintain balances. In the so-called consultation breakfast , Bergara recalled the importance of understanding the signs of the world to face responsibly the pressures on the economy mainly through the flow of capital that puts pressure on the exchange rate. In his presentation, called "That this intertwined world does not glimpse us ( )", the president of the BCU recalled that the financial markets were in a state of exuberance and "fortunately some corrections are starting to happen." "Every moment there is noise, capital takes refuge in the dollar, conditioned by global expectations ," said the president of the BCU. In turn, he exemplified that currently the novelty of cryptocurrencies does nothing more than add volatility to the markets, which represents an "element of concern for regulators at the international level," he said. In this sense, he explained the importance of maintaining exchange rate flexibility with intervention criteria based on not going against fundamentals, monitoring global developments, reducing volatility and preventing excessive appreciations or depreciations. The president of the BCU showed optimism regarding the behavior of the Uruguayan economy mainly due to domestic demand and exports, which show growth of around 10%. In the fiscal field, Bergara ratified the sustainability of the debt (around 30% net of GDP) and with a growth perspective of the economy estimated at around 3%-3.5% for this year. In that scenario, he recalled that international analysts maintain their perception about Uruguay's financial strength . However, the president of the BCU reviewed several challenges that the country has ahead. Among them, he mentioned that the growth of the economy is not reflected in improvements in employment levels. In this regard, he explained that this variable operates with lag with respect to economic evolution; partly as a result of technological dynamics. Regarding inflation, he ratified as healthy the concern generated in society by a rise like that of February, since this collaborates with the work carried out by the Central Bank. "We welcome the concern, because it shows that society has matured this issue a lot after half a century of double- and triple-digit inflation . It is easier for the Central Bank to explain its work with a more conscious society," he said. He also pointed out that "we have price stability and a lot of capacity of agents to navigate with inflation. like the current one without altering their economic decisions." However, he said that work must continue based on the fact that the inflation expectation of the agents continues around 7% (ceiling of the target range). In that sense, he recalled that the focus of economic policy is to meet multiple objectives, with greater emphasis on some, but "without drama" with respect to none.

Para el Banco Central es ms fcil explicar su trabajo con una sociedad ms consciente, sostuvo. Title: The president of the BCU explained to investors the logic of Uruguay in the face of the normalization of financial conditions
text: IV International Investment Conference The president of the BCU explained to investors the logic of Uruguay in the face of "the normalization of financial conditions" The president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara, assured Latin American investors that Uruguay is well prepared to face the current economic cycle due to the risk management approach that economic policy applied in the last decade. In that sense, he showed what are the two current challenges for the authorities: international volatility and the processes derived from the economic cycle. "The current conditions are lived as a process of normalization of economic conditions at the international level," Bergara explained to 200 businessmen gathered at the IV International Investment Conference that was held. at the Hotel Casino Carrasco in Montevideo. In this scenario, the president of the BCU reasoned that economic policy prepared the circumstances to navigate that change in the global and regional situation. "Much of what happens we do not see as the world coming down, we see it as a process of normalization of financial conditions," emphasized the president of the BCU. Faced with this new context, Bergara reviewed the strengths of the free floating of the dollar, which allows it to match its international trend, in contrast to what happened in past decades when the rupture of the exchange rate parity schemes ended with hyperinflation. "The current inflation of 10% is already processing the nominal exchange rate depreciation of 35%," Bergara exemplified, adding that this figure represents a central concern of economic policy. Interventions in the foreign exchange market by the Central Bank are one of the actions that soften the fluctuations of the dollar and collaborate in price stability. Likewise, these interventions in recent months had a positive effect on the BCU's debt management, since the reduction of reserves by 4,000 million dollars implied a decrease in the BCU's debt by 6,000 millions of dollars. On the other hand, the president of the Central Bank warned that international volatility feeds back into the economic cycle and therefore recalled the need to maintain a balance in economic policy objectives . Among them, he mentioned fiscal policy, which in Uruguay maintains a clear signal of adequacy of the deficit according to what the approved Budget Law shows. For Bergara, Uruguay's risk management policy and behavior allow a positive perception to be maintained by investors and risk rating agencies. "In a context where many countries lose their credit rating and investment grade , Uruguay has a solid position in terms of credit rating," he emphasized. In fact, between 2014 and 2015 Uruguay was one of the two countries in the world (along with Slovakia) that improved their credit rating after obtaining investment grade. The president of the BCU closed by recalling that this adequate and reasonable platform allows to navigate a "turbulent world", generating conditions of tranquility for those who bet on Uruguay with productive and financial investment. "The history of credibility, respect for contracts and compliance with obligations consolidates and solidifies that perception of investment grade that exists with respect to the Uruguayan economy," Bergara concluded. The IV International Investment Conference organized by Compass Group analyzed in Montevideo the behavior of Latin American and global markets and the economic prospects for the region. Para Bergara, la poltica de administracin de riesgos y el comportamiento de Uruguay permite mantener una percepcin positiva por parte de inversores y calificadoras de riesgo. En un contexto donde muchos pases pierden su calificacin crediticia y el grado inversor, Uruguay tiene una posicin slida en cuanto a la calificacin crediticia, enfatiz. La historia de credibilidad, respeto de contratos y cumplimiento de obligaciones consolida y solidifica esa percepcin de grado inversor que existe respecto a la economa uruguaya, concluy Bergara. Title: This world makes the dollar move with extreme volatility
text: IV Cooperative Summit of the Americas Bergara: "This world makes the dollar move with extreme volatility" This was indicated by the president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara, who made a presentation this afternoon about the economic situation of the country, the region and the world in the framework of of the IV Cooperative Summit of the Americas. The exhibition was held in the Conference Room of the Radisson Montevideo Hotel and was attended by representatives of cooperativism from all over the continent, among which were the main referents of the Uruguayan Confederation of Cooperative Entities. Bergara began by expressing that "the BCU must have a sense of belonging to the society for which it works" and in this sense stressed the need to "strengthen ties with everyone. the agents that make up the social fabric". The president of the BCU said that "today we are in a context of economic slowdown and with the characteristic that developed countries have a mediocre growth perspective ." He reiterated that uncertainty and volatility characterize these times and that "the electoral result in the US reaffirms it." "This world makes the dollar move with extreme volatility," a variable that he described as absolutely relevant in regional economies . However, he indicated that commodity prices have acted as a counterpart to the eventual strengthening and weakening of the dollar. Bergara explained that China, the main partner of the countries of the region, continues to grow at considerable rates and has not stopped demanding food, so those who export it They have not been as harmed as those who produce in other areas. He pointed out that in the Uruguayan case work was done to mitigate vulnerabilities since "China growing at rates of 8%, prices through the clouds of commodities and a dollar for the soil, they couldn't last forever." "In the long run rates will rise and the dollar will strengthen, but at the moment the world is very volatile and political and economic events are constantly happening that do so. reflect," he said. For the president of the Central Bank , the necessary response in this context is an economic policy that aims at price stability, financial and public accounts. Title: Bergara: The Central Bank does not evaluate professionals but the transactions they report
text: October 26, 2016 Bergara: "The Central Bank does not evaluate professionals but the transactions they report" The president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara, said today that the focus of compliance with the new obligations to combat money laundering and financing of terrorism is on the transactions and not on the professionals who present the Suspicious Transaction Reports (ROS). This comment was made during a presentation before lawyers and scribes who attended the Academic Week of the Institute of Commercial Law of the Faculty of Law of the University of the Republic. The conference was called "On corporate, banking and tax transparency ( - %20Presentation%20Institute%20Right%20Commercial.pdf)" and reviewed the new global regulatory requirements and changes being processed in Uruguay. In that sense, the president of the Central Bank made it clear that the establishment of limits to obligations for professionals is the task of legislative discussion. Precisely, in his opinion, the new regulatory projects will have the objective of drawing the line between the duty of reservation of the professional (under certain circumstances) and the obligation to report suspicious transactions. It should be noted that the BCU has already carried out training instances with notaries and other subjects obliged to submit this type of report. "We want professionals to internalize this problem and report more fluently," Bergara said. At the same time, he contextualized that these changes occur in the face of the need for regulatory adaptation for the prevention of money laundering and the new international taxation, which will result in a path towards little or no opacity in this terrain. The president of the BCU recalled that Uruguay will undergo the evaluation of the Financial Action Task Force of Latin America (GAFILAT) in 2019 and will join the commitment of automatic multilateral exchange of tax information of OECD in 2017 and 2018. A possible consequence of this process will be the erosion of the bank secrecy regime. The legislative proposal to consider the tax crime as a precedent for laundering, the registration of final beneficiaries of national companies and trusts are examples of this regulatory adaptation that implies moving towards the elimination of the innominativity of shares (bearer shares), Bergara summarized. Title: Speech about the economic situation in the Economics Course for Union Leaders
text: August 29, 2016 The president of the BCU presented on the economic situation in the Economics Course for Trade Union Leaders The president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara, gave a seminar on the economic situation, which is part of the Economics Course for Trade Union Leaders organized together with the Institute of Economics of the Faculty of Economic Sciences and Administration and with the support of the Cuesta Duarte Institute of the PIT-CNT. This course aims to contribute to the improvement of the understanding of economic and financial issues by trade union leaders in their capacity as agents of intermediation between workers, employers and the State. To do this, the program addresses the issues of economics and finance using a everyday language to present and analyze cases of the national economy. The objective is to provide participants with tools to understand the macroeconomic situation, incorporate microeconomic fundamentals and understand the functioning of markets. Among the topics covered in the course are economic indicators, the labor market, the exchange rate, inflation, monetary policy and fiscal policy. This training initiative is part of the functions entrusted to the BCU in its Organic Charter, in terms of strengthening the capacities for economic and financial decision-making of the population, which it carries out through the BCUEduca Program.

Para ello, el programa aborda los temas de economa y finanzas utilizando un lenguaje cotidiano para presentar y analizar casos de la economa nacional. El objetivo es dotar a los participantes de herramientas para entender la coyuntura macroeconmica, incorporar fundamentos microeconmicos y comprender el funcionamiento de los mercados. Entre los temas tratados en el curso se destacan los indicadores econmicos, el mercado de trabajo, el tipo de cambio, la inflacin, la poltica monetaria y la poltica fiscal. Title: Uruguay navigates volatility in a reasonable way, but we are not complacent
text: June 13, 2018 Mario Bergara: "Uruguay navigates volatility in a reasonable way, but we are not complacent" Uruguay reasonably navigates global volatility, in a world that imposes challenges on the Uruguayan economy, so "we do not even have a self-congratulatory situation," said the president of the Central Bank of Uruguay. (BCU), Mario Bergara, before businessmen gathered at a working breakfast convened by Somos Uruguay. Since its tasks, the Central Bank has acted in a countercyclical manner and with a flexible monetary policy given the movements of the exchange rate in the country, where it is easy to move from one currency to another for significant amounts," he said. According to the president of the BCU, the volatility of the dollar at the global level is explained by geopolitics and is reinforced by the logic of expectations, with the context of the region as an additive. In that sense, he analyzed that the political framework in Brazil is uncertain, with difficulties in visualizing how it will emerge from a complex situation, among other reasons due to problems of legitimization of the political system. Likewise, in the economic field that country has not shown signs that it will have a growth that allows it to sustainability. In the case of Argentina, the president of the BCU stressed that Argentina's growth expectations cooled again given the economic imbalance and social problems. According to Bergara, the shocks coming from the global economy put to the test the platform and risk management strategy that Uruguay has had. "In the commercial and financial field there is less exposure to the region," he said. Among the attributes of the domestic economy, the president of the BCU listed economic growth at decent rates, the recovery of domestic demand, the healthy evolution of exports of goods and services and the current account surplus of the balance of payments. He also stressed that the country has an orderly fiscal framework, guided by the need for adaptation, but "not from the drama," said Mario Bergara in his conference called "Uncertain world and turbulent region: and by house how are we doing? ( )". In the course of the presentation, he recalled that the fiscal framework appears as orderly, but guided by the need for adaptation. "We are in time to make an adjustment taking advantage of the growth of the economy, maintaining the objectives explicit by the government in investment and public spending, but adapting the result to consolidate that sustainable trajectory of the public accounts, which has been explicit in the formulation of Accountability," he said. In the same way, the president stressed that growth has not yet led to improvements in employment levels, which is why he reiterated the need that exists in the country to reactivate the investment process. In this sense, he recalled that Uruguay has consolidated its investment grade to such an extent that although there are challenges the country is well positioned and that is reflected when the country makes placements in the financial markets. From the commercial and financial point of view, the country has to insert itself into a complex world and in the process, Uruguay has much to gain, because today hundreds of millions of dollars of tariffs are paid. "You have to talk about trade agreements and then decide based on the interests of the country; what you can't make say is this I'm not talking about," said the president of the BCU.

En el caso de Argentina, el presidente del BCU subray que las expectativas de crecimiento de Argentina se volvieron a enfriar dado el desbalance econmico y los problemas sociales. A juicio de Bergara, los shocks provenientes de la economa global ponen a prueba la plataforma y estrategia de manejo de riesgos que ha tenido Uruguay. En el terreno comercial y financiero hay menor exposicin a la regin, dijo. Entre los atributos que tiene la economa domstica, el presidente del BCU enumer el crecimiento econmico a tasas decentes, la recuperacin de la demanda domstica, la saludable evolucin de las exportaciones de bienes y servicios y supervit de la cuenta corriente de la balanza de pagos. Tambin remarc que el pas cuenta con un marco fiscal ordenado, pautado por la necesidad de adecuacin, pero no desde el dramatismo, sostuvo Mario Bergara en su conferencia denominada Mundo incierto y regin turbulenta: y por casa cmo andamos? (http://www.bcu.gub.uy/Comunicaciones/Conferencias/Somos_Uruguay_2018.pdf). En el transcurso de la exposicin record que el marco fiscal aparece como ordenado, pero pautado por necesidad de adecuacin. Del mismo modo, el presidente remarc que el crecimiento an no arrastra a mejoras en los niveles de empleo, por lo cual reiter la necesidad que existe en el pas de reactivar el proceso inversor. En este sentido, record que Uruguay ha consolidado su grado de inversin a tal punto que si bien existen desafos el pas est bien posicionado y eso se refleja cuando el pas hace colocaciones en los mercados financieros. Desde el punto de vista comercial y financiero, el pas tiene que insertarse en un mundo complejo y en el proceso, Uruguay tiene mucho para ganar, porque hoy se pagan cientos de millones de dlares de aranceles. Hay que hablar sobre acuerdos comerciales y luego decidir en base a los intereses del pas; lo que no se puede hacer decir es de esto no hablo, remarc el presidente del BCU. Title: The president of the BCU sees that banks will have the capacity to adapt to the challenges posed by fintech
text: December 7, 2016 The president of the BCU envisions that banks will have the capacity to adapt to the challenges posed by fintech The president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara, envisions that banks will have the capacity to adapt to the challenges posed by the emergence of financial platforms, known as fintech. Bergara presented as a guest at the conference "Telecommunications, the new world of means of payment", organized by the Uruguayan Chamber of Telecommunications. In the perspective of the president of the Central Bank, "fintech (contraction of the English words finance and technology) will be taken advantage of by the current intuitions in the adaptation process and, therefore, these platforms will not cause a drastic displacement of agents in the current system." However, Bergara stressed that there is a challenge, a reduction in profitability opportunities, although logically, banks and other agents will adapt using fintech with the aim of reducing their costs. The president of the BCU reflected that the very existence of banks is given by the existence of information asymmetries, which are challenged by financial platforms. However, Bergara differentiated that these technological platforms aim at financing consumption or carrying out transactions of reduced amounts at the level of families and have not yet managed to establish themselves as intermediaries in operations where regulation is necessary. contractual. "The contractual risk of operations of this type is enormous and no matter how much information costs are reduced , there is another part of information asymmetries that this technological change cannot replace," Bergara said. Likewise, the president of the Central Bank pointed out that the other challenge is that of regulation, where it is necessary to re-understand why it is regulated and put the focus where it is really needed. The regulator must be concerned with protecting the uninformable while minimizing the systemic risk of the banking and financial system, the BCU president concluded.

Title: Mario Bergara: Reality shows a relationship between financial inclusion and economic development
text: October 19, 2016 Mario Bergara: "Reality shows a relationship between financial inclusion and economic development" The president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara, reflected on the importance of economic and financial education to promote healthy behaviors based on greater access to financial services by increasing sectors of society. "Using financial services must go hand in hand with financial education, they are two sides of the same coin," Bergara said during his presentation "Inclusion and financial education: two sides of the same coin" ( ) ", which he made invited by a group of students from UTU's Management courses. In that sense, he cited research that shows that countries with financial inclusion are those with economic development. Therefore, Bergara stressed the importance of deepening the use of the financial system due to its positive effects on economic, human and social development. Bergara recalled that currently in Uruguay there is a need to improve access to these services among micro, small and medium-sized enterprises as well as families with lower incomes and, therefore, the State takes the initiative to promote financial inclusion. For it to work, one of the necessary milestones that the president of the Central Bank recalled was the modernization of the payment system. This involves moving from payments through banknotes, coins and checks that are expensive to print and transfer, to debit, credit and wire card transactions. This system is "more efficient, transparent, secure and cheap," Bergara emphasized, reminding students that "electronically you can have a greater follow-up of personal finances." In the same way, these mechanisms allow to generate a culture of savings, for example for the purchase of housing, he added. However, for everything to work, education has a central role since it allows to generate healthy habits when making economic and financial decisions in daily life, said the president of the BCU. Title: Speech about the economic situation before businessmen in Rivera
text: June 15, 2016 The president of the BCU spoke about the economic situation before businessmen in Rivera The president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), Mario Bergara, spoke about issues of economic situation before businessmen and merchants in the north of the country, invited by the Association of Merchants and Industrialists of Rivera (ACIR). The conference called "Ni sobrerreaccion, ni paralysis: staying the course ( ) ", developed at the headquarters of ACIR, had an outstanding presence of its associates, who knew in detail the vision of the BCU in relation to the economic situation of the country, the region and the world. The president of the BCU explained that the global economic situation presents challenges such as a slowdown, strengthening of the dollar and a fall in international prices, all of them "foreseeable phenomena of the economic cycle". In that regard, he pointed out that Uruguay is no stranger to this situation. "Volatility and uncertainty is the current feature of markets," he stressed. Regarding the reduction in the price of commodities, he said that the fall for Uruguay is not significant due to the items it exports. "In some cases what is not exported to certain destinations, is reorientable to others," he said, referring to the 140 destinations in which the country sells its products. According to Bergara, in the regional environment both Brazil and Argentina present an unfavorable combination in terms of their main macroeconomic variables such as inflation, fiscal deficit and growth. In that sense, he highlighted the construction of a platform already proven by Uruguay, which "continues to be useful to navigate these times." Bergara referred to a "currency depreciation" as important as that of previous periods, but with other effects. He underlined the solid financial position of the country and the banking system, in addition to the first place that Uruguay occupied at the end of 2015 in the recognized Latinobarometro index in terms of citizen satisfaction with the economy. With regard to inflation, he reaffirmed that "it is a priority objective of economic policy." In this regard, he said that "the economic policy of the BCU is being very contractionary, as it can not be otherwise." The president of the BCU insisted once again with the approach of economic policy that allows to maintain the course: exchange rate flexibility that "softens volatility", adequacy of income to the process of economic slowdown, debt management that mitigates financing risks and the maintenance of investment grade as a relevant asset. On this last point, he pointed out the solid credit rating that Uruguay holds and that ratifies the strengths of the economy.

Title: Speech at the National Academy of Economy: It is important that we converge expectations to the inflation range
text: President of the BCU at the National Academy of Economics: "It is important that we converge expectations to the inflation range" The president of the Central Bank of Uruguay (BCU), economist Diego Labat, said that monetary policy will maintain the expansive mood required by the current health emergency context beyond the fact that the BCU has begun a transition path towards the use of the interest rate instrument announced by the last Monetary Policy Committee. This, because he added that in the current situation of the health emergency, the maintenance of the expansive phase of monetary policy allows money restrictions to be avoided. "The transition to an interest rate regime requires an intermediate operational implementation process," said the president of the monetary authority during a videoconference held on August 13, invited by the National Academy of Economics of Uruguay. In his presentation entitled "Strategy of the Monetary Policy of the Central Bank of Uruguay", which was followed virtually by analysts, academics, former government ministers who are part of the National Academy of Economics, as well as representatives of the media, Labat explained that "the use of the rate represents a better signal to the market for a better reading by agents". The presentation of the president of the BCU also exhibited the Central Bank's agenda for the coming years where, according to him, the focus should be on anchoring inflation expectations to the target range. "As long as this does not happen, we have to be critical," he said. And he recalled that "the inflation target of these years was very high; we do not come out well, we are in the top 13% of the highest inflation worldwide" which represents "a poor record". To reverse this situation, economist Labat argued that it is key that each policy is linked to a policy objective, that at the same time they are consistent with each other, with adequate coordination to consolidate a path of credibility. In the absence of greater independence of the Central Bank, it is necessary to coordinate macroeconomic policies consistent with each other and in which each institution strictly complies with its mandate, this coordination being the main element for building credibility. And he announced that in September the Macroeconomic Coordination Committee will meet where each of the tasks of each of the policies will be explained, respecting the independence of each institution. "Once the different agents begin to see the consistency of fiscal and income policy, credibility will emerge in monetary policy and the announcements of the Central Bank," he stressed. The presentation made by the president of the Central Bank reviewed at the beginning the diagnosis and the agenda prior to the Covid-19 coronavirus pandemic; the BCU's performance during the health emergency; emerging challenges; the measures adopted; its results and future plans. At the present time, guided by the health emergency declared on March 13, 2020 due to the Covid-19 coronavirus, Labat recalled that the financial system was called to be part of the solution, where in his opinion the industry was up to the task, dialogue has flowed and solutions have always been sought. "Monetary policy was put into an expansive phase to contemplate the need for low rates, while a greater emphasis on controlling inflation was announced once the emergency was overcome to control inflation expectations," he reviewed. There he listed among the measures adopted the reduction of reserve requirements to facilitate credit; the extension of credit terms, the facilities in the calculation of guarantee and the facilitation of procedures, among other decisions adopted by the institution. In this sense, he graphically showed that the financial system used a third of the money that the BCU made available through a reduction in the reserve regime. At the conference, Labat, who also referred to the financial system and financial stability, mentioned that in his initial diagnosis he saw that there was financial stability on the one hand, but at the same time he observed that there were challenges to be developed: "We had a very good starting point for the financial system in terms of stability, but also pending issues for Uruguay to make a leap in quality." The future agenda of the Central Bank also includes the strengthening of the regime of primary operators, completing the agenda of transparency of monetary policy, work to specify a path towards de-dollarization and, in the longer term, the presentation of a discussion on the institutionality of monetary policy.
